[1mFour words steer the tutor:[0m

[1;97mSTAGE 1 — Where am I?[0m

Five short lessons (about 10 minutes) followed by a small task.
You'll meet the prompt, run a few simple commands, and learn the
keyboard habits that make the shell easy to live with.

[93m▶ Type [92mnext[93m to start lesson 1.1.[0m

[1;97mRunning commands[0m

At the prompt below, type this and press Enter:

  [92mecho hello[0m

You'll see [90mhello[0m printed, then the prompt comes back. Now try:
  [92mecho I am at the shell[0m      [90m# spaces separate words[0m
  [92mecho "I am at the shell"[0m    [90m# quotes group them into one[0m

If bash says [92mcommand not found[0m or [92mNo such file[0m, you mistyped: a stray
[92m/[0m in front, or a missing space. Type it again.
[92mecho[0m just repeats its words back. It is the simplest command
there is, and its shape is the shape of every command you'll meet:
a name, then the words you hand it.

[93m▶ Try all three, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m
echo I am at the shell
echo I am at the shell

[1;97mKeyboard habits[0m

Four keys make the shell comfortable. Try each one now.

  [1mTab[0m       bash finishes a word. Several matches? The first [1mTab[0m
            fills in the shared part; [1mTab[0m again lists them. (Other

shells and setups differ.) Try: type [92mecho p[0m, press [1mTab[0m;
            it becomes [92mecho poem.txt[0m, then press Enter to run it.
  [1m↑[0m         brings back the last line. Enter runs it; [1mCtrl+C[0m throws it away.
  [1mCtrl+L[0m    clears the screen ([92mclear[0m too); [92mshow[0m brings the lesson back.
  [1mCtrl+C[0m    the escape hatch at a prompt: if a command feels stuck,
            press it and you get a fresh prompt. Inside a full-screen
            program like [92mless[0m (Stage 3), [1mq[0m is the way out.

[93m▶ Try each key, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m

[1;97mWhere am I, who am I, when is it[0m

Three commands that ask the system about itself.

  [92mwhoami[0m     [90m# the user name you're logged in as[0m
  [92mpwd[0m        [90m# print working directory — the folder you're in[0m
  [92mdate[0m       [90m# the current date and time[0m

Here [92mpwd[0m shows the tutor's own folder, because that is where
this practice prompt starts. Stage 2 is all about folders.

Your prompt here ends in [92m>[0m. A normal bash window's prompt
usually ends in [92m$[0m; same idea, different decoration.

[93m▶ Run all three, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m

[1;97mThe shell, caught in the act[0m

Type [92mdate[0m. Now type [92mdtae[0m.

  [92mdate[0m     [90m# prints the date and time[0m
  [92mdtae[0m     [90m# bash: dtae: command not found[0m
Read who is speaking. [92mbash:[0m is the shell. It looked for a
program called dtae, found none, and told you. When the name is
right, it finds the program and runs it; what the program prints
comes back to you.
Three parts, kept apart for the rest of this tutor:
  [1mterminal[0m  →  [1mshell[0m  →  [1mprogram[0m
The terminal is the window. The shell is the program named [92mbash[0m
that read your line. [92mdate[0m is the program it ran.

[93m▶ Try both, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m

[1;97mWho else types here[0m

Everything you typed went terminal → shell → program. There is no
other way in: anything that runs a command on this machine goes
through a shell the same way.

An AI assistant that "runs commands" for you is no exception. It
types a line into a shell; the shell finds the program; the program
runs. The line it typed can be read exactly as you read your own.

So the habits in this course count twice:
  [1mread the line[0m before anyone presses Enter — you, or a helper
  [1mknow the folder[0m it will run in

[1mread the output[0m when it comes back, instead of skimming it

[1;97mSTAGE 2 — Paths and the filesystem[0m

Four lessons, then a gate. The shell is always [1msomewhere[0m in
the filesystem; this stage teaches you to see where, look around,
move, and predict where files land.

You'll use:
  [92mpwd[0m   print where you are now

[92mls[0m    list what's in the current folder
  [92mcd[0m    change to another folder
And the path symbols:
  [1m.[0m     this folder
  [1m..[0m    the parent folder
  [1m~[0m     your home folder

[93m▶ Type [92mnext[93m to begin lesson 2.1.[0m

[1;97mWhere you are[0m

A folder can hold files and other folders. You are always standing
in one folder; the shell calls it the [1mcurrent directory[0m.
Your practice folder looks like this:

  /var/folders/jx/f_4n055973x5cwnyh_mhlw9h0000gn/T/shelltutor-sim-home-bcn3vvmt[0m  [93m◀ you are here[0m
  ├── poem.txt

└── stage2/

[92mpwd[0m prints the name of the current directory.
Predict what it will print, then run it.

[93m▶ Run [92mpwd[93m, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m

[1;97mls: what is here[0m

[92mls[0m lists the names in the current directory.

[92mls -p[0m         [90m# folders end in /[0m
  [92mls -a[0m         [90m# also hidden names: those starting with .[0m

Predict which names will end in [92m/[0m, then run [92mls -p[0m. The
tutor keeps its own hidden files here; [92mls -a[0m shows them.

Then [92mls[0m a folder you are not in:
  [92mls /[0m          [90m# the top of everything[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin[0m   [90m# long: many commands live here[0m

[1;97mcd: moving[0m

[92mcd[0m changes your current folder.

  [92mcd /tmp[0m       [90m# go to /tmp[0m

  [92mcd[0m            [90m# your home folder, outside this practice area[0m
  [92mcd ~[0m          [90m# also your home folder (~ is its short name)[0m
  [92mcd -[0m          [90m# come back to where you were[0m
  [92mcd ..[0m         [90m# go up one level (to the parent folder)[0m
[92mcd..[0m with no space is a different word; bash cannot find it.

[1;97mNames for places[0m

Three short names point at places in the tree you have seen:
  [1m.[0m    here, the current directory
  [1m..[0m   one level up, the parent
  [1m~[0m    your home folder

A [1mpath[0m names a place. [1mRelative[0m paths start where you are:
  [90mpractice/notes.txt[0m   a file inside a subfolder
  [90m../notes.txt[0m         a file in the parent folder

[1mAbsolute[0m paths start from the root, [1m/[0m:
  [90m/etc/hosts[0m   [90m/usr/bin/vim[0m
[91mPredict before you act.[0m  In [90m~/projects[0m, the bare name [90mnotes[0m means [90m~/projects/notes[0m.
  [92mmkdir name[0m    [90m# make a folder called name, right here[0m

[1;97mSTAGE 3 — Files and operations[0m

Three lessons, then a gate. You'll create, read, copy, move, and remove
files. [91mrm is immediate.[0m It does not move things to a trash.
We'll do everything inside /var/folders/jx/f_4n055973x5cwnyh_mhlw9h0000gn/T/shelltutor-sim-home-bcn3vvmt/stage3[0m so practice is
contained.
Commands this stage:
  [92mtouch[0m   create an empty file (or update its timestamp)
  [92mmkdir[0m   create a folder

[92mrmdir[0m   remove an EMPTY folder
  [92mcat[0m     print a text file
  [92mless[0m    page through a long file (exit with [1mq[0m)
  [92mcp[0m      copy
  [92mmv[0m      move (or rename — same command)
  [92mrm[0m      remove a file ([91mimmediate[0m)

[93m▶ Type [92mnext[93m to begin lesson 3.1.[0m

[1;97mCreating: touch, mkdir[0m

[92mtouch[0m creates an empty file (or updates the timestamp of
an existing one).
  [92mtouch hello.txt[0m
  [92mls[0m              [90m# you should see hello.txt[0m

[92mmkdir[0m creates a folder.

[92mmkdir notes[0m
  [92mls[0m              [90m# notes/ is now there[0m

To put words in a file, send [92mecho[0m's output into it (more on [92m>[0m in Stage 4):
  [92mecho hello > notes.txt[0m   [90m# put words in a file[0m
So: [92mtouch[0m for empty files, [92mmkdir[0m for folders, [92m>[0m for words.

[93m▶ Make a few, put a word in one, then [92mnext[93m.[0m

[1;97mReading: cat, less[0m

[92mcat[0m prints the entire file at once.
  [92mcat hello.txt[0m                [90m# probably empty[0m
  [92mcat ../poem.txt[0m        [90m# the tutor's poem, one folder up[0m

For a long file, [92mcat[0m floods the screen. Use [92mless[0m
to page through it:

[92mless ../numbers.txt[0m    [90m# 50 lines — more than one screen[0m
Inside [92mless[0m, the screen takes over. Press [1mSpace[0m
or [1mf[0m to page down, [1mb[0m to page back, and
[1mq[0m to exit. (More on full-screen programs in Stage 5.)
[91mImportant:[0m when [92mless[0m takes over, the prompt is
gone. You're inside a program. [1mq[0m returns you to the shell.

[93m▶ Try both; [1mq[93m leaves [92mless[93m; then [92mnext[93m.[0m

The terminal is a quiet room.
You speak to it, it answers back.
Words have shapes here, and shapes have weight.
A pipe is a doorway between rooms.

[1;97mCopy, move, delete[0m

[92mcp[0m copies. The original stays.
  [92mcp hello.txt backup.txt[0m

[92mmv[0m moves; the same command [1mrenames[0m:
  [92mmv hello.txt hi.txt[0m            [90m# rename[0m
  [92mmv hi.txt notes/[0m               [90m# move into a folder[0m

[92mrm[0m deletes. [91mImmediately and permanently.[0m
  [92mrm backup.txt[0m
There is no Trash and no undo. [91mLook before you press Enter —
you, or an assistant typing for you.[0m
[1mA safety habit[0m: [92mls[0m first, then [92mrm <only-now-that-you-are-sure>[0m.

[1;97mSTAGE 4 — Commands, streams, composition[0m
Four lessons, then a gate. You'll read a command's structure, check
whether a command exists, and chain commands together with pipes,
redirects, and globs.
Commands this stage:

[92mcommand -v[0m   ask the shell if a program is installed
  [92mwc[0m           word, line, and character count
  [92mseq[0m           generate number sequences
  [92mhead[0m          first N lines of input
  [92msort[0m          sort lines
  [92mgrep[0m          select lines matching a pattern
  [92m|[0m             [1mpipe[0m: send one command's output into the next
  [92m>[0m             [1mredirect[0m: write output to a file (overwrites)
  [92m>>[0m            [1mappend[0m: add output to the end of a file

[93m▶ Type [92mnext[93m to begin lesson 4.1.[0m

[1;97mReading a command[0m

A shell command has a small grammar:
  [1mcommand  options  arguments[0m

[92mls -l /etc[0m               [90m# option + argument[0m
  [92mwc -l poem.txt[0m           [90m# count lines in a file[0m
  [92mecho "hello world"[0m       [90m# an argument with a space — quoted[0m
[91mSpaces matter.[0m  The shell splits on spaces; [1mquote[0m a name that has one:
  [92mvim "my notes.txt"[0m       [90m# opens one file[0m
  [92mvim my notes.txt[0m         [90m# opens TWO files: 'my' and 'notes.txt'[0m
[1mcommand -v[0m asks the shell whether a command exists:
  [92mcommand -v ls[0m            [90m# prints the path; exits 0[0m
  [92mcommand -v vim[0m           [90m# does Vim exist on this system?[0m

[93m▶ Try a few [92mcommand -v[93m probes, then [92mnext[93m.[0m

[1;97mThe pipe[0m

A [1mpipe[0m ( [92m|[0m ) sends one command's output into the next command's
input. [91mMost important idea in the shell.[0m

[92mwc[0m counts [1mwhatever you piped in[0m:
  [92mwc -l poem.txt[0m          [90m# lines in poem.txt[0m
  [92mseq 1 100 | wc -l[0m       [90m# 100[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin | wc -l[0m     [90m# how many programs are installed[0m

Pipes stack:
  [92mls /usr/bin | sort | head[0m        [90m# list → sort → first 10[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin | grep ^a[0m            [90m# names starting with 'a'[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin | grep ^a | wc -l[0m    [90m# …and count them[0m
Each piece is a normal command; only the connector is new. [92m|[0m is Shift+Backslash.

[1;97mRedirection[0m

A pipe sends output to [1manother program[0m. A redirect sends it
to [1ma file[0m, and [92m>[0m replaces it without asking, whoever typed the line.

  [92m>[0m    write to a file ([91moverwrites[0m if it exists)

[92m>>[0m   append to a file (creates if missing)
  [92m<[0m    read a file [1minto[0m a command
  [92mecho first > greeting.txt[0m        [90m# overwrite[0m
  [92mecho second >> greeting.txt[0m      [90m# append[0m
  [92mcat greeting.txt[0m                 [90m# two lines[0m
  [92mwc -w < poem.txt[0m                 [90m# count words read from poem.txt[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin | sort > programs.txt[0m     [90m# a pipe and a redirect together[0m
  [92mwc -l programs.txt[0m

[93m▶ Try them, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m

[1;97mGlobs[0m

[1mGlobs[0m match many filenames at once. The shell expands them
[1mbefore[0m the command sees them.

  [92mls *.txt[0m              [90m# every .txt file in this folder[0m
  [92mwc -l *.txt[0m           [90m# count lines in each .txt file[0m

[92mcat *.txt[0m             [90m# print them all back-to-back[0m

[91mPredict before you act.[0m  [92mrm *[0m removes everything
in the current folder. [92mrm *.tmp[0m removes only .tmp files.

[1;97mBuffer vs file[0m

[91mThe most important idea in this stage.[0m When you open a file in
Vim, Vim [1mreads it into a buffer[0m — a copy in memory. Your
keystrokes change the [1mbuffer[0m, not the file. The file on disk
only changes when you [1mwrite[0m the buffer back.

  [1mfile on disk[0m  →  [1mbuffer in memory[0m  →  [1mfile on disk[0m
       (read)                  (edit)                     (write)
That's why Vim has separate commands for save and quit:
  [92m:w[0m    write the buffer to the file
  [92m:q[0m    quit (only if there are no unsaved changes)
  [92m:q![0m   quit and discard unsaved changes
  [92m:wq[0m   write, then quit
